scope.repairFocus: Ambiguous data-planning key, duplicate distractor, sleep-scenario alignment, and item-specific evidence-appraisal explanations.

revisedOptions: Prioritize extra speed work because the 30-m time is squad-median
Interpret the 30-m rank alongside fatigue, asymmetry, and rugby demands
Treat the athlete's best sprint score as the complete profile and plan
List results without priorities or follow-up measures for training
changes.reviewerNote: Made the integration option uniquely best by contrasting it with an unjustified speed-only response to a median sprint result.

revisedOptions: Perform maximal intervals to chase fatigue before sleep
Test adaptation with another strength session
Repeat maximal training to test immediate tolerance
Use a low-intensity walk with normal recovery habits
changes.reviewerNote: Replaced a semantic duplicate distractor with a distinct high-intensity tolerance-testing error.

changes.revisedText: A young athlete sleeps poorly after late training and struggles to learn new tactical patterns. Which explanation is most defensible?
changes.reviewerNote: Removed the contradictory adequate-sleep condition so the keyed sleep-learning explanation matches the scenario.

changes.revisedExplanation: Random allocation creates assigned programmes that can be compared through the difference in return-to-running outcomes, subject to adherence and uncertainty.
changes.reviewerNote: Replaced the generic explanation with an RCT-specific assigned-group outcome contrast.

changes.revisedExplanation: Randomly assigned carbohydrate and placebo groups provide the intervention contrast used to compare cycling-test outcomes.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the trial-specific assigned carbohydrate/placebo contrast.

changes.revisedExplanation: Random allocation permits estimation of the outcome contrast between assigned technique training and usual training, rather than a self-selection association.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the randomized technique-training/usual-training contrast.

changes.revisedExplanation: The trial compares outcomes under the two assigned exercise doses; blinded assessment helps reduce outcome-assessment bias but does not change the assigned-group contrast.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the assigned dose contrast and explained the role of blinded assessment.

changes.revisedExplanation: Random assignment creates two hydration-strategy groups whose core-temperature outcomes can be contrasted while accounting for uncertainty and adherence.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the trial-specific hydration-strategy contrast.

changes.revisedExplanation: The central RCT comparison is reaction time under assigned sleep coaching versus the assigned usual routine, not a self-selected sleep association.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the assigned sleep-coaching/usual-routine comparison.

changes.revisedExplanation: A prospective cohort classifies or records weekly load without random assignment and examines its association with later player outcomes.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the prospective exposure and later-outcome association specific to the cohort item.

changes.revisedExplanation: The cohort observes baseline sleep duration and follows athletes for later respiratory illness, estimating an association rather than a randomized effect.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the sleep-exposure and later-illness follow-up rationale.

changes.revisedExplanation: Recorded travel exposure precedes follow-up for muscle complaints, so the design can examine their association but cannot claim a randomized travel effect.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the observed travel exposure and later-complaint association rationale.

changes.revisedExplanation: The registry observes home-exercise adherence and later return-to-running time, estimating an observational association that may be confounded by adherence-related factors.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the adherence exposure and return-to-running follow-up rationale.

changes.revisedExplanation: The cohort compares observed recovery-room use with later illness, so it estimates an association rather than a randomized preventive effect.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the observed recovery-room exposure and later-illness association rationale.

changes.revisedExplanation: Baseline low-energy-availability indicators are followed against later bone-stress injury, allowing an association to be examined without randomizing energy availability.
changes.reviewerNote: Added the baseline indicator and later-injury follow-up rationale.

changes.revisedExplanation: Substantial loss to follow-up can create attrition bias and reduce precision, so the large effect must be judged for missing outcomes and rehabilitation applicability.
changes.reviewerNote: Named attrition bias, precision, missing outcomes, and applicability tested by the item.

changes.revisedExplanation: An unvalidated fatigue score threatens measurement validity, while a single-club sample and imprecision limit how confidently the finding transfers to other athletes.
changes.reviewerNote: Named validation, sampling bias, precision, and applicability concerns specific to the wearable study.

changes.revisedExplanation: Omitted prior injury and exposure timing can confound the load–injury association; measurement quality and applicability must also be appraised.
changes.reviewerNote: Named confounding, timing, measurement quality, and applicability tested by the cohort item.

changes.revisedExplanation: Very different protocols and outcomes create heterogeneity and question whether pooling is meaningful, alongside bias and relevance of the review.
changes.reviewerNote: Named compatibility, heterogeneity, bias, and relevance concerns specific to the pooled review.

changes.revisedExplanation: A poorly reported comparator, adherence, and confidence interval weaken interpretation of the warm-up claim and require critical appraisal before application.
changes.reviewerNote: Named comparator, adherence, uncertainty, and study-design concerns specific to the prevention claim.

changes.revisedExplanation: Frequent missing data and one-team sampling can introduce selection bias and reduce transferability, so precision and missingness must be considered.
changes.reviewerNote: Named missing-data, selection-bias, precision, and transferability concerns specific to the wearable paper.
